h1: Brewing a Belgian blonde ale at home
title: Brewing a Belgian Blonde Ale at Home | Craft Beer School
desc: A Belgian blonde ale homebrew recipe for 20 litres with grist, hops, yeast and the fermentation schedule that gives a dry, spicy, golden beer.
teaser: Strong, golden and dangerously easy to drink. A Belgian blonde rewards careful fermentation more than fancy ingredients.
standfirst: Belgian blonde ale is golden, around 6 to 7.5% ABV, dry and gently spicy from its yeast. The recipe is simple. The skill is in the sugar, the mash and above all the fermentation temperature.
sections: What a Belgian blonde should taste like

The BJCP style guidelines, which most homebrew competitions judge against, describe a Belgian blond ale as moderately strong, golden and dry. The usual numbers are an original gravity of 1.062 to 1.075, a final gravity of 1.008 to 1.018, 6.0 to 7.5% ABV and 15 to 30 IBU. Colour sits at pale gold.

In the glass it should be bright with a dense white head. The aroma mixes light fruit, a soft spice from the yeast and a hint of honeyed Pilsner malt. It finishes dry, so the strength hides well. A blonde is gentler and less bitter than a tripel and lighter in colour than a dubbel. If you enjoy witbier, our guide to brewing a Belgian witbier covers its spicier cousin.

For a 20 litre batch at about 72% brewhouse efficiency, aiming for an OG near 1.066:

  • 4.6 kg Pilsner malt (84%)
  • 0.3 kg Munich malt (5%)
  • 0.6 kg plain white sugar, added in the boil (11%)

Hops: Styrian Golding or Saaz for bitterness at 60 minutes to reach about 22 IBU, plus a small charge of the same hop at 10 minutes. Belgian blonde is not a hoppy beer, so keep late hops modest.

The sugar is not a shortcut. It ferments completely, which lightens the body and keeps the finish dry at this strength. Indian white sugar works perfectly. Belgian candi sugar is not needed for a pale beer.
Mash low for a dry finish

Mash at 64 to 65 °C for 60 to 75 minutes. That favours beta amylase and gives a highly fermentable wort. A warmer mash leaves more body and sweetness, which is the wrong direction for this style. Pilsner malt can carry more of the compound that becomes dimethyl sulphide, so give the wort a vigorous 90 minute boil with the lid off. Our mash temperature guide explains how each degree shifts fermentability.

Water should be soft to moderate. Indian borewell water is often very hard. If yours is, cut it with RO water or packaged drinking water to keep the beer crisp.
Yeast and temperature make the beer

Use a Belgian abbey or blonde strain, either dried or liquid. Pitch generously. A high gravity Belgian beer needs plenty of healthy yeast. Two 11 g packets of dried yeast or a good starter for liquid yeast is about right for 20 litres at 1.066.

Temperature is where most homebrew Belgians go wrong. Start cool, at 18 to 19 °C, for the first two or three days. The yeast makes most of its flavour in this growth phase, so a cool start keeps fusel alcohols down. Then let the temperature rise to 22 to 24 °C to help the yeast finish dry. In Indian heat the danger is the opposite of most places: an uncontrolled start at 28 °C produces harsh, hot alcohol. Start cool with a fridge or water bath and let it warm later.

Belgian blondes are lively. Aim for about 2.5 to 3 volumes of carbon dioxide. That is higher than a standard ale, so use strong bottles. Avoid thin, reused one-trip bottles for anything above about 2.7 volumes. Condition at 20 to 24 °C for two to three weeks, then store cool.

The beer improves with a few weeks of cold conditioning as the yeast character softens and the flavours knit together. Serve at 6 to 8 °C in a tulip glass or goblet to show off the head and aroma. The same strength that makes it pleasant also makes it easy to underestimate, so pour smaller measures than you would for a session beer.

This recipe works. Making it taste genuinely Belgian takes control of yeast health, pitch rate and temperature profile, the details that separate a clean blonde from a hot, solventy one. Learning to steer the yeast through those changes is the core of Belgian brewing. If you enjoy experimenting with sugars, our guide to brewing a honey ale with Indian honey covers another fermentable that dries the finish.

Your first step: before brew day, set up a way to hold the fermenter at 18 °C for the first three days. A tub of water with frozen bottles swapped twice a day is enough to start.
faqs: What yeast should I use for a Belgian blonde?
A Belgian abbey or blonde ale strain. Pitch plenty of it and start fermentation cool, around 18 to 19 °C.
Why add sugar to a Belgian blonde?
Sugar ferments completely, which lightens the body and keeps the beer dry and drinkable at 6 to 7.5% ABV.
How strong is a Belgian blonde ale?
Usually 6.0 to 7.5% ABV, according to BJCP style guidelines.
